section_summary: This section documents United States diplomatic observations and intelligence from March 1938 through May 1939 regarding political developments and ministerial reorganizations within the Japanese Cabinet. It covers the May 1938 reconstruction of Prince Fumimaro Konoe's Cabinet designed to intensify the prosecution of the war in China, the internal government clash over the establishment of a centralized China Affairs Board (Kōain / Tai Shi In) which precipitated the resignation of Foreign Minister Kazushige Ugaki in September 1938, and the eventual resignation of the entire Konoe Cabinet in January 1939. The records trace the subsequent formation of the nationalist Hiranuma Cabinet, subsequent ministerial appointments including General Kuniaki Koiso and Harumichi Tanabe in April 1939, and international reactions to Japanese cabinet instability from London, Moscow, and Chungking.

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting the compromise creation of the China Economic Affairs Bureau and the China Economic Inquiry Commission under Cabinet supervision.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on the compromise reached between the Cabinet Legislative Bureau and the Foreign Office regarding administrative control over China affairs. The Cabinet decided on March 14 to establish the China Economic Affairs Bureau under Cabinet direction to supervise development companies without handling diplomatic matters, alongside a China Economic Inquiry Commission headed by the Premier. Foreign Minister Hirota firmly opposed an overarching political and cultural board outside the Foreign Office, arguing it would infringe Chinese sovereignty and antagonize foreign powers.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2827: Creation of China Economic Affairs Bureau and China Economic Inquiry Commission

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting inside information that the Konoe Cabinet is about to be reconstituted to prosecute the China conflict more vigorously.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits confidential information from a prominent Japanese close to Prime Minister Konoe indicating an imminent Cabinet reconstitution to satisfy elements demanding a more aggressive China policy. Konoe is expected to remain in office while Hirota is expected to be replaced by General Ugaki, with Hiranuma considered as an adviser. Grew notes that an issue of the Asahi Shimbun discussing these changes was suppressed by government censors, confirming the substance of the report.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 330: Anticipated Reconstitution of the Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram announcing the new Japanese Cabinet appointments for Foreign Affairs, Finance, Commerce and Industry, and Education.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew sends an urgent plain message reporting the Cabinet appointments announced on the afternoon of May 26, 1938. General Kazushige Ugaki is appointed Minister for Foreign Affairs, Seishin Ikeda receives the concurrent portfolios of Finance and Commerce and Industry, and General Sadao Araki is named Minister of Education. Detailed political commentary is promised in a following message.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 332: Announcement of Japanese Cabinet Appointments

subfiles.about: Telegram analyzing the political alignment of the reconstructed Cabinet and impending leadership changes in the War Ministry.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew analyzes the Cabinet shakeup, reporting that the government now represents all positivist elements united in prosecuting the China conflict. War Minister Sugiyama and Vice Minister Umezu are expected to step down in favor of Generals Itagaki and Tojo. The report clarifies that Hirota's replacement stemmed from his close association with Sugiyama's faction, while business leader Ikeda and General Ugaki have committed to the continental program while offering stabilizing domestic and foreign influence.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 335: Further Analysis of Japanese Cabinet Reconstruction

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a Tokyo despatch reporting on changes within the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet records Tokyo Despatch No. 2975 dated May 31, 1938, filed under decimal file 894.00/796. The despatch transmits detailed reports concerning internal ministerial changes and appointments within the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Tokyo Despatch No. 2975 regarding Changes within the Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a telegram reporting that Toshio Shiratori's appointment as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs is unlikely to materialize.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Tokyo Telegram No. 438, sent at 2 p.m. on July 5, 1938, and originally filed under 894.00/802. It reports that the rumored appointment of nationalist diplomat Toshio Shiratori as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs was unlikely to occur because of anticipated unfavorable reactions in the United States and Great Britain.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Tokyo Telegram No. 438 regarding Proposed Appointment of Shiratori

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a Moscow despatch reporting Soviet press coverage on the reorganization of the Japanese Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Moscow Despatch No. 1370 dated June 16, 1938, originally filed under 761.94/1063. The despatch transmits Soviet press commentaries interpreting the Japanese Cabinet reorganization as an indicator of internal weakness and mounting difficulties arising from Japan's military campaign in China.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Moscow Despatch No. 1370 regarding Soviet Press Comments on Japanese Cabinet Reorganization

subfiles.about: Telegram interpreting the Cabinet reconstruction as a victory for Konoe's aggressive war policy over Sugiyama's conservative strategy.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides an extensive evaluation of the May 26 Cabinet reconstruction, characterizing it as a triumph for Premier Konoe and advocates of aggressive warfare over General Sugiyama's faction. The reorganization was reportedly delayed until the capture of Hsuchow (Xuzhou) to safeguard national prestige and avert a military uprising. The new lineup balances moderates such as General Ugaki and financier Seishin Ikeda with ardent militarists such as Araki and Suetsugu, uniting diverse elements to prosecute the China incident with increased vigor.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 333: Significance and Complexion of Japanese Cabinet Reconstruction

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a London despatch transmitting British press comments on the Japanese Cabinet changes.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Despatch No. 430 dated May 28, 1938, from the American Embassy in London, filed under 894.00/794. The despatch transmits British press reporting and editorial commentary on the recent reconstruction of the Japanese Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: London Despatch No. 430 regarding British Press Comment on Japanese Cabinet Changes

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a telegram reporting the appointment of General Itagaki as War Minister and the resignation of General Sugiyama.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Tokyo Telegram No. 352, sent at 7 p.m. on June 3, 1938, and originally filed under 894.00/793. It officially reports the resignation of General Hajime Sugiyama and the appointment of General Seishiro Itagaki as Minister of War.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Tokyo Telegram No. 352 regarding Appointment of General Itagaki as War Minister

subfiles.about: Extract from Tokyo political report reviewing Cabinet friction over China policy, Konoe's illness, and vernacular press criticism.
subfiles.summary: This extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 3020 (Political Report No. 125) reviews Cabinet tensions during April 1938 concerning military and economic strategy toward China. A fundamental policy dispute existed between Premier Konoe, who favored decisive destructive operations, and War Minister Sugiyama, who advocated economic exhaustion through a prolonged war. Following a three-week illness, Konoe resumed duties on April 21 reaffirming the January 16 non-recognition policy, but faced criticism from the vernacular press regarding Cabinet disunity and his physical fitness.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3020 (Extract): Cabinet Policy on Sino-Japanese Conflict and Premier Konoe's Resumption of Duties

subfiles.about: Extract from Tokyo political report detailing the May 1938 Cabinet shakeup, ministerial appointments, and policy declarations.
subfiles.summary: This extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 3089 (Political Report No. 126) provides a comprehensive review of the May 26 Cabinet reorganization, detailing the replacements of Hirota, Kaya, Yoshino, and Kido. It notes the subsequent appointment of General Tojo as Vice Minister of War and reports General Ugaki's instructions to the armed services to conduct military operations in China without diplomatic hesitation. It also quotes Education Minister Araki's ideological policy statement emphasizing imperial virtue and character training.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3089 (Extract): Reorganization of the Konoe Cabinet in May 1938

subfiles.about: Extract from Tokyo political report covering General Itagaki's assumption of office, the five-minister conferences, and Araki's educational outlook.
subfiles.summary: This extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 3094 (Political Report No. 127) covers General Itagaki's appointment as War Minister and the transfer of the Overseas portfolio to General Ugaki following Sonyu Otani's departure to head the North China Development Company. It outlines the establishment of the Five-Minister conferences to coordinate national policy and war supplies, Konoe's remarks foreshadowing a new Imperial Conference, and an interview with Education Minister Araki professing dedication to pacific internationalism.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3094 (Extract): Assumption of Office by General Itagaki and the Five-Minister Conferences

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a telegram reporting the resignation of Foreign Minister Ugaki over jurisdictional conflict regarding the China board.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Tokyo Telegram No. 635, sent at 8 p.m. on September 29, 1938, and filed under 894.00/814. It reports that Foreign Minister Kazushige Ugaki submitted his resignation due to an irreconcilable conflict between the Foreign Office and the Army over administrative jurisdiction of the proposed China board.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Tokyo Telegram No. 635 regarding Resignation of Foreign Minister Ugaki

subfiles.about: Telegram detailing the resignation of Foreign Minister Ugaki, Konoe's assumption of his duties, and the dispute over the China organ.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports the acceptance of General Ugaki's resignation and Premier Konoe's temporary assumption of the Foreign Affairs and Overseas portfolios, alongside the resignation of diplomatic advisers Sato and Arita. The breakdown occurred at a five-minister conference where Ugaki flatly rejected Army demands for an independent China agency vested with administrative authority over occupied areas, arguing it violated the constitution and ruined foreign relations. Grew concludes that the core problem remains deep division among Japanese leaders regarding continental policy following the January 16 declaration.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 636: Circumstances Surrounding Foreign Minister Ugaki's Resignation

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a despatch on the proposed establishment of the China Board (Tai Shi In) and Ugaki's resignation.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Tokyo Despatch No. 3300 dated October 4, 1938, filed under 894.00/819. It addresses the proposal to create the China Board (Tai Shi In) as the catalyst for General Ugaki's resignation, Five-Minister conferences, and Prince Konoe's positions on the organ's structure.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Tokyo Despatch No. 3300 regarding the China Board (Tai Shi In) and Ugaki's Resignation

subfiles.about: Extract from Tokyo political report analyzing the prolonged Cabinet controversy over the central China organ and press reaction to Ugaki's departure.
subfiles.summary: This extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 3308 (Political Report No. 130) reviews the protracted debate over creating a central organ for China affairs, identifying it as the foremost destabilizing issue within the Konoe administration. The Army's comprehensive scheme sought to preempt Foreign Office prerogatives over diplomacy, trade, and economic development companies in China, prompting Ugaki's constitutional objections. The vernacular press widely lamented the lack of political cohesion, with the Tokyo Nichi Nichi contrasting it unfavorably with the spirit of conciliation demonstrated by European statesmen at Munich.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3308 (Extract): Controversy over the Central China Organ and Resignation of Foreign Minister Ugaki

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a despatch on Ugaki's resignation and the difficulty of finding a career diplomat to head the Foreign Ministry.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Tokyo Despatch No. 3320 dated October 7, 1938, filed under 894.00/818. It discusses Foreign Minister Ugaki's opposition to the China Board (Tai Shi In) and observes the improbability of finding an acceptable career diplomat willing to accept the Foreign portfolio before the status of the board is finalized.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Tokyo Despatch No. 3320 regarding Foreign Minister Ugaki's Resignation and the China Board

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a telegram reporting the appointments of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister and Yoshiaki Hatta as Overseas Minister.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Tokyo Telegram No. 691, sent at 1 p.m. on October 29, 1938, and filed under 894.00/820. It reports the formal appointments of Hachiro Arita as Minister for Foreign Affairs and Yoshiaki Hatta as Minister for Overseas Affairs.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Tokyo Telegram No. 691 regarding Cabinet Appointments of Arita and Hatta

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a State Department memorandum regarding the appointment of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records an internal memorandum written by Mr. Schuler of the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs on October 29, 1938, filed under 894.00/821. The memorandum comments on the political significance of Hachiro Arita's return to the post of Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: State Department Memorandum on Appointment of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing an Albania despatch reporting the appointment of Toshio Shiratori as Minister to Tirana and Ambassador to Rome.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Despatch No. 743 dated October 12, 1938, from the American Legation in Tirana, Albania, filed under 701.9475/3. It notes that Japanese diplomat Toshio Shiratori was appointed Minister to Albania and concurrent Ambassador to Italy.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Albania Despatch No. 743 regarding Appointment of Toshio Shiratori

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a Tokyo despatch reporting on the appointment of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Tokyo Despatch No. 3392 dated November 1, 1938, filed under 894.00/822. It indexes Ambassador Grew's formal report and political observations regarding Hachiro Arita's assumption of the office of Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Tokyo Despatch No. 3392 regarding Appointment of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister

subfiles.about: Extract from Tokyo political report covering the appointments of Arita, Hatta, Horinouchi, and Sawada, and Japan's immutable China policy.
subfiles.summary: This extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 3424 (Political Report No. 131) details Cabinet and diplomatic changes following Ugaki's resignation. Premier Konoe temporarily held the Foreign portfolio before relinquishing his extra posts on October 29 with the appointment of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister and Yoshiaki Hatta as Overseas Minister, while Kensuke Horinouchi was designated Ambassador to Washington and Renzo Sawada became Vice Minister. The report notes that Arita fully supports Japan's fixed continental policy and will press Western powers to recognize the new situation in East Asia.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3424 (Extract): Cabinet Changes and Diplomatic Appointments in October 1938

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the installation of Baron Hiranuma as Prime Minister and Prince Konoe's entry as Minister without portfolio.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports radio announcements confirming that Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma was installed as Prime Minister on the evening of January 5, 1939. Prince Konoe succeeded Hiranuma as President of the Privy Council while remaining in the Cabinet as Minister without Portfolio. Most key members of Konoe's inner Cabinet (Arita, Itagaki, Yonai) remain in office, with the major exception of Finance Minister Seishin Ikeda who resigned.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 9: Installation of Baron Hiranuma as Prime Minister

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a telegram reporting the installation of new officers in the Hiranuma Cabinet and press reaction.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Tokyo Telegram No. 14, sent at 6 p.m. on January 6, 1939, and filed under 894.00/833. It reports the installation of new ministers in the Hiranuma Cabinet, summarizes official statements, and analyzes press coverage that discounted notions of a political crisis while highlighting Hiranuma's ideological orientation.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Tokyo Telegram No. 14 regarding Resignation of Konoe Cabinet and New Appointments

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a telegram reporting late December political maneuvering, rumors of Konoe's replacement, and peace feelers toward Wang Ching-wei.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Tokyo Telegram No. 813, sent at 7 p.m. on December 29, 1938, and originally filed under 894.00/826. It reports heightened political tension in Tokyo, widespread rumors regarding Prime Minister Konoe's resignation, possible cabinet reorganization, and secret contacts with Wang Ching-wei concerning a definite peace proposal.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Tokyo Telegram No. 813 regarding Political Situation and Rumored Resignation of Konoe

subfiles.about: Urgent telegram reporting the resignation of the entire Japanese Cabinet on the morning of January 4, 1939.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits an urgent rush message stating that the entire Japanese Cabinet under Prime Minister Prince Fumimaro Konoe submitted its resignation on the morning of January 4, 1939.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 4: Resignation of the Entire Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram detailing press forecasts regarding personnel carryovers and ministerial vacancies in the incoming Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details newspaper forecasts concerning the new Cabinet lineup following Konoe's resignation. Itagaki, Shiono, and Kido are slated to enter the new administration, while Suetsugu, Ikeda, Arima, Nagai, and Nakajima are definitely excluded. If Baron Hiranuma is selected as Premier, Konoe will succeed him as President of the Privy Council, with Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal Yuasa dispatched to secure Prince Saionji's approval.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 5: Projected Lineup of the Incoming Japanese Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram evaluating Konoe's public statement and the growing ascendancy of authoritarian governance under Hiranuma.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew analyzes Prince Konoe's noon announcement explaining his resignation. Konoe stated that having led the government through major hostilities, the transition to the second phase of the conflict—domestic and continental political reconstruction—required renewed public confidence under fresh leadership. Grew interprets the transition to Baron Hiranuma as evidence that Konoe was unable to stem the tide toward an authoritarian regime.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 6: Konoe's Explanation for Resignation and Rise of Authoritarianism

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a State Department memorandum on the significance of the Konoe Cabinet's resignation.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records a memorandum written by Joseph W. Ballantine of the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs on January 4, 1939, filed under 894.00/851. The memorandum assesses the political significance and international implications of the resignation of Prince Konoe and his Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: State Department Memorandum on Significance of Konoe Cabinet Resignation

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Chinese press commentary from Chungking interpreting the Japanese Cabinet collapse as a sign of weakness.
subfiles.summary: Peck transmits summaries of Chungking Chinese press reactions to the fall of the Konoe Cabinet. The journals interpret the resignation as a symptom of mounting Japanese internal strain and economic exhaustion, while cautioning that the incoming reactionary Hiranuma Cabinet will accelerate aggressive military moves. The Central Daily News and Ta Kung Pao note that the collapse signals militarist desperation and nullifies Wang Ching-wei's peace overtures, while the Sao Tang Pao predicts friction with Russia and stronger ties with the European Axis.
subfiles.title: Chungking Telegram No. 16: Chinese Press Reactions to the Fall of the Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram summarizing Soviet press coverage and a Pravda article analyzing the Japanese political crisis and Hiranuma's fascist orientation.
subfiles.summary: Kirk summarizes Soviet reporting on the Japanese government crisis, highlighting an analytical article by Koroliov in Pravda titled 'The New Government in Japan.' The analysis attributes Konoe's downfall to the failure of his China strategy, rising anti-war sentiment, and international isolation resulting from lack of financial support from Berlin and Rome. Pravda portrays Hiranuma as a champion of fascist militarism serving nobility and monopoly capital, predicting accelerated aggression in East Asia alongside persistent domestic economic dilemmas.
subfiles.title: Moscow Telegram No. 12: Soviet Press Reactions to Cabinet Reorganization in Japan

subfiles.about: Extract from Tokyo political report on the failure of the national reorganization movement and late December rumors of Konoe's replacement.
subfiles.summary: This extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 3615 (Political Report No. 133) reviews political developments during December 1938, focusing on the proposed totalitarian movement for the reorganization of the nation. The plan encountered stiff resistance from the Minseito and Seiyukai parties who feared liquidation, while Home Minister Suetsugu lost enthusiasm and Premier Konoe grew dissatisfied, culminating in the Cabinet's decision to postpone the scheme. The report recounts persistent year-end rumors proposing Konoe's replacement by General Minami, Baron Hiranuma, or Marquis Kido amid widespread public weariness.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3615 (Extract): Political Crisis and Postponement of National Reorganization Plan

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a Tokyo despatch transmitting the membership roster of the new Hiranuma Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Tokyo Despatch No. 3600 dated January 13, 1939, filed under 894.00/844. It indexes the formal diplomatic report transmitting the complete list of ministers installed in the new Cabinet headed by Prime Minister Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma on January 5, 1939.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Tokyo Despatch No. 3600 regarding Membership of the New Hiranuma Cabinet

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a Moscow despatch transmitting translations of Soviet press comment on the Japanese Cabinet change.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Moscow Despatch No. 2020 dated January 18, 1939, originally filed under 894.00/842. The despatch transmits English translations of Soviet newspaper articles analyzing the political significance of the change of Cabinet in Japan.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Moscow Despatch No. 2020 regarding Soviet Press Comment on Japanese Cabinet Change

subfiles.about: Extract from Tokyo political report providing the official roster of the Hiranuma Cabinet and analyzing the causes of Konoe's resignation.
subfiles.summary: This extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 3656 (Political Report No. 134) provides the official ministerial roster of the Hiranuma Cabinet installed on January 5, 1939. Major carryovers included Kido, Itagaki, Yonai, Arita, Araki, and Shiono, with Konoe becoming Minister without Portfolio and Privy Council President, while Ikeda and Suetsugu departed. The Embassy attributes Konoe's resignation to Cabinet division over Suetsugu's strict national regimentation measures, Diet opposition, and a widespread public yearning for fresh leadership during the reconstruction phase of the China conflict.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3656 (Extract): Installation and Roster of the Hiranuma Cabinet

subfiles.about: Document file note referencing a despatch on the appointments of General Koiso as Overseas Minister and Harumichi Tanabe as Communications Minister.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Tokyo Despatch No. 3815 dated April 11, 1939, filed under 894.00/853. It reports the appointments of General Kuniaki Koiso (retired) as full-time Minister for Overseas Affairs and Harumichi Tanabe as Minister of Communications.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Tokyo Despatch No. 3815 regarding Appointments of General Koiso and Harumichi Tanabe

subfiles.about: Extract from Tokyo political report detailing the backgrounds of General Koiso and Tanabe, and planned changes in Commerce and Industry.
subfiles.summary: This extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 3912 (Political Report No. 137) reviews the investiture on April 7, 1939, of General Kuniaki Koiso as Overseas Minister and Harumichi Tanabe as Communications Minister, relieving Hatta and Shiono of concurrent duties. It highlights Koiso's expansionist background in Manchuria and Korea, his Kokuhonsha ties, and his calls to strengthen the Anti-Comintern Pact with Germany and Italy while placing Japanese industry on a total war footing. It also details Tanabe's technical experience in communications and Manchukuo, noting administrative reorganization plans for the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3912 (Extract): Cabinet Appointments of General Koiso and Harumichi Tanabe
